subject: physics
question_text: Explain reversible and irreversible processes. Describe the working of Carnot engine. Obtain an expression for the efficiency.

verification.note: Asked in TS March 2017 (Q21), March 2019 (Q21) and March 2025 (Q21) — TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, Section C, 8 marks each time. The five-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: the cycle is isothermal expansion at T₁ (A→B), adiabatic expansion (B→C), isothermal compression at T₂ (C→D), adiabatic compression (D→A); for one mole Q₁ = RT₁ ln(V₂/V₁) and Q₂ = RT₂ ln(V₃/V₄); the adiabatic relations TV^(γ−1) = constant applied to B→C and D→A give V₂/V₁ = V₃/V₄, so the two logarithms cancel and η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Reversible and irreversible
lines: A reversible process can be made to run
backwards through the same states, so that at
the end the system and the surroundings are
both back in their starting conditions.
It must be quasi-static (very slow) and free
of friction, viscosity and every other loss.
An irreversible process does not retrace its
path. Free expansion of a gas, heat flow
across a large temperature difference and any
process with friction are irreversible.
All natural processes are irreversible. A
reversible process is an ideal limit.
steps.margin_note: First two marks. One for the definition with both conditions, one for the contrast plus examples.
steps.why: The Carnot cycle is built out of reversible steps only, so this part is not a preface — it is the assumption the efficiency formula rests on.
common_mistakes: Saying a reversible process only returns the SYSTEM to its starting state. The surroundings must return as well.
Leaving out the two conditions. Quasi-static and loss-free are what make a process reversible.

recall.must_convey: That a reversible process retraces the same states and returns both system and surroundings to their starting conditions, needs to be quasi-static and loss-free, and that all natural processes are irreversible.

steps.memory_tip: Reversible needs BOTH back: the system and the surroundings, by the same path.

steps.label: The Carnot cycle on a P–V diagram
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Letter the four states A, B, C, D, put an arrow on each step, and mark T₁ and T₂ on the two isotherms.
steps.why: The derivation below is written off this diagram: V₁ to V₄ are the volumes at A, B, C and D, and the two isotherms are the only steps that exchange heat.
common_mistakes: Drawing the adiabats less steep than the isotherms. An adiabat is always the steeper of the two through a given point.
Leaving the arrows off. Without them the same drawing is a refrigerator.

recall.must_convey: That the answer needs a P-V diagram with two isotherms, two adiabats, the states A, B, C, D and arrows showing the direction of the cycle.
accept: draw the P V diagram of the cycle
mark A B C D with arrows
reject: Q one is R T one log V two by V one

steps.memory_tip: Adiabats are the steeper pair. A to B and C to D are the flatter isotherms, at T₁ and T₂.

steps.label: The four processes
lines: A Carnot engine uses an ideal gas working
between a source at T₁ and a sink at T₂.
1. A → B: isothermal expansion at T₁. The gas
takes heat Q₁ from the source.
2. B → C: adiabatic expansion. No heat enters
or leaves and the gas cools to T₂.
3. C → D: isothermal compression at T₂. The
gas rejects heat Q₂ to the sink.
4. D → A: adiabatic compression. The gas
warms back to T₁ and the cycle closes.
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. All four steps, in order, each named isothermal or adiabatic with its temperature.
steps.why: Heat is exchanged on the isothermal steps only, so naming which two steps are adiabatic is what allows Q₁ and Q₂ to be written for the isothermal steps alone.
common_mistakes: Starting with the adiabatic expansion. The cycle begins with the isothermal expansion at T₁.
Saying the temperature changes on an isothermal step. The gas stays at T₁ or at T₂; the temperature changes only on the adiabatic steps.

recall.must_convey: The four steps in order: isothermal expansion at T one taking Q one, adiabatic expansion cooling to T two, isothermal compression at T two rejecting Q two, adiabatic compression back to T one.
accept: takes Q one at T one and rejects Q two at T two
reject: a reversible process retraces its path

steps.memory_tip: Expand twice, then compress twice, alternating isothermal and adiabatic each time.

steps.label: Heat taken and rejected
lines: For one mole of an ideal gas the work in an
isothermal step equals the heat exchanged:
The adiabatic steps exchange no heat, so the
net work in the cycle is W = Q₁ − Q₂ and
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Both heats with the correct volume ratios, and the efficiency written as 1 − Q₂/Q₁.
steps.why: On an isothermal step the internal energy of an ideal gas does not change, so the first law makes the heat exchanged equal to the work done. That is why both heats reduce to a logarithm of a volume ratio.
common_mistakes: Writing Q₂ = R T₂ ln(V₄/V₃) and getting a negative value. Q₂ is written as the heat REJECTED, so the larger volume V₃ goes on top.
Adding the adiabatic steps into Q₁ or Q₂. No heat crosses the boundary on an adiabatic step.

recall.must_convey: That Q one is R T one log of V two by V one, Q two is R T two log of V three by V four, and eta is one minus Q two by Q one.
accept: Q one is R T one log V two by V one
Q two is R T two log V three by V four
eta is one minus Q two by Q one
reject: V two by V one equals V three by V four
heard_as: R T log V two by V one
one minus Q two by Q one

steps.memory_tip: Both heats have the form R × T × ln(larger V / smaller V).

steps.label: The efficiency
lines: Apply the adiabatic relation TV^(γ−1) =
constant to the two adiabatic steps:

lines.text: B → C:  T₁ V₂^(γ−1) = T₂ V₃^(γ−1)
D → A:  T₁ V₁^(γ−1) = T₂ V₄^(γ−1)

lines: Dividing the first by the second gives
so ln(V₂/V₁) = ln(V₃/V₄). The two logarithms
cancel in the ratio Q₂/Q₁:

lines.text: Q₂/Q₁ = T₂ ln(V₃/V₄) / T₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = T₂/T₁

steps.margin_note: The last two marks. One for the two adiabatic relations and the division, one for the final formula.
steps.why: Once the logarithms cancel, the efficiency depends on the two temperatures alone and on nothing about the gas or the size of the engine. That is the result the whole derivation is for.
common_mistakes: Writing η = 1 − T₂/T₁ straight after the diagram. The two adiabatic relations and the division are where the marks are.
Putting the temperatures in degrees Celsius. T₁ and T₂ are absolute temperatures in kelvin.

recall.must_convey: That the adiabatic relation applied to both adiabatic steps and divided gives V two by V one equal to V three by V four, so the logarithms cancel and eta is one minus T two by T one.
accept: T V to the power gamma minus one is constant
V two by V one equals V three by V four
eta is one minus T two by T one
reject: Q one is R T one log V two by V one
heard_as: one minus T two by T one

steps.memory_tip: Divide the two adiabatic relations: the volume ratios come out equal and the logarithms cancel.

insider_note: The two logarithms cancelling is worth 2 of the 8 marks and is where most answers stop. Write both adiabatic relations first.
